extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies, sociology, and philosophy interested in Bergson's theory of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Bergson's account of what provokes the comic and the social function of laughter, including its causes (rigidity, absent-mindedness), social role (discipline/ridicule), and aesthetic preferences (visual over verbal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity / mechanical behaviour as cause of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson argued that laughter is provoked by rigid or mechanical behaviour — 'the attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine' and 'the comic is "something mechanical encrusted on the living"'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a pedestrian failing to dodge an obstacle; an absent-minded professor dipping his pen into glue where his inkwell normally stands. The comic arises specifically from human behaviour appearing non-elastic or machine-like; incongruity theories are insufficient because they don't explain which incongruities produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of absent-mindedness correlates with degree of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent-mindedness is 'always comical' and 'the deeper the absent-mindedness the higher the comedy' — Bergson treats absent-mindedness as a form of rigidity that heightens the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more pronounced the failure of memory/preparedness for action (e.g., elegant but unaware gestures), the more comical the result; this links to his examples from theatrical comedy where graceful execution combined with absent-mindedness intensifies laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a disciplinary corrective (social function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions to discourage inelastic behaviour and to maintain social adaptability: 'rigidity is the comic, and laughter is its corrective'. Society holds the prospect of being laughed at as a deterrent against inflexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disciplinary function ties cause (rigidity) to effect (ridicule) designed to prevent repetition; without such ridicule society risks ossification. This is presented as a necessary social function rather than merely a surplus pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of humiliation/pain for corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: For laughter to operate as a corrective it must make 'a painful impression on the person against whom it is directed' — the humiliation is an intended part of its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson argues laughter cannot 'bear the stamp of sympathy or kindness' if it is to intimidate and correct; the cruelty/humiliation element is thus functional and (arguably) necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure of laughter mixed with a secret/unavowed intent to humiliate
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter's pleasure is 'not an unadulterated pleasure' but 'always implies a secret or unconscious intent' — an 'unavowed intention to humiliate' that may be unconscious or disavowed by the laugher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translators' rendering carries Freudian resonance; Bergson implies an unconscious, potentially sadistic component to laughing that sociologically functions as discipline but psychologically involves self-deception and pleasure in humiliating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social (communal) rather than purely psychological function
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson prioritizes the social role of laughter over psychological release theories: humour 'fulfils a social rather than a psychological function', explaining why communal laughter often exceeds individual laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions operate 'behind the back' of social actors — people do not consciously laugh to correct others; the social analyst attributes functions that actors themselves may not recognise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of the visual/bodily over the verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson gives priority to visual, wordless, bodily humour (slapstick, gestures): many of his comic prototypes are 'wordless', and bodily gesture counts for more than scripted wit in his account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-class theatrical comedy still privileges constructed character and gesture; modern media (film/TV close-ups) can convey subtle gesture well (e.g., Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Office). Bergson downgrades verbal jokes/puns relative to bodily comic situations because language fixes categories and reduces lived variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity of comic misfortune (only misfortunes from inelasticity are funny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all misfortunes are comic; misfortune is comic when it results from inelastic or non-adapted behaviour (making the person look stupid), whereas many misfortunes are tragic rather than comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comedic quality depends on the nature of the misfortune: those revealing rigidity/absent-mindedness produce laughter; other types do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality claim grounded in natural disposition to find rigidity comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson's theory accounts for humour's universality by assuming humans are constituted to find rigidity comic in order to promote social adaptability and elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rigidity threatens adaptation, laughter's disciplinary role is portrayed as universally beneficial to social life; this supports a claim that humour has a necessary function across societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between conservative/disciplined and innovative/subversive roles of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tension in Bergson's theory: laughter's disciplinary (conservative) role may suppress innovation, yet humour can also be recruited in the service of radicalism; Bergson prioritises the conservative function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: the Paris magazine Le Rire sided with innovators, while Punch policed bourgeois norms; Bergson acknowledges both possibilities but gives theoretical priority to ridicule as enforcing social rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of the comic on social norms, manners and prejudices (insociabilité)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unsociability' (insociabilité) — behaving out of tune with others' expectations (speaking too loudly, dressing flamboyantly, etc.) — often forms the basis for ridicule; the comic is 'so frequently dependent on the manners or ideas, or to put it bluntly, on the prejudices of society'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everyday codes of politeness are moralized; failing them can make one a comic figure in fiction and a target of criticism in real life. Thus what is laughed at varies with cultural norms and prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap between function and conscious experience (unconscious operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional explanations of laughter posit effects operating without conscious intent: 'The social significance of laughter is not to be found within the conscious experience of the person who is laughing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should distinguish the function (social correction) from actors' stated reasons; laughter often occurs spontaneously without an explicit corrective motive in awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and conceptual categories limit detection of comic subtleties
rubrics_metrics.description: Language 'intervenes between [the thing] and ourselves' and reduces inner states to impersonal categories; Bergson distrusts language for masking the individual, fleeting qualities that make situations comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because words fix categories, verbal humour may be limited in capturing the unique lived particulars that Bergson values; philosophers should 'look behind language' to intuit reality beyond labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical/metaphysical framing: comic as manifestation of spirit vs matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson connects the comic to his broader metaphysics: the comic shows the 'spirit' (élan vital) struggling against inert matter; excessive machine-likeness (matter) diminishes the spirit and becomes risible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour thus functions to protect the creative spirit and promote evolution/adaptation by discouraging rigid, mechanical reproduction of behaviour; this is a metaphysical rationale rather than an empirical test.
